ai.title: Compact ID generator uses 64-bit base64url
ai.summary: generateCompactId now produces 64-bit identifiers using 40 timestamp bits and 24 random bits, encoded as base64url (~11 chars). Replaces the previous 32-bit base36 scheme (~5-6 chars) to reduce collision risk and ensure URL safety. Updated in common/src/util/string.ts. Bitwise operations use BigInt to preserve full 64-bit precision.

eli5.text: When you create a new link or reference code in this system, it now generates a longer but much safer identifier, about 11 characters instead of 5 or 6. The new format combines a timestamp and random data using a URL-friendly encoding so links are far less likely to clash with each other. You would notice the IDs look different (more characters, different letters and numbers) and work better in web addresses without needing cleanup. This is live today for anyone using the compact ID feature.

ai.title: generateCompactId drops BigInt
ai.summary: generateCompactId in common/src/util/string.ts replaces BigInt arithmetic with native Number operations for timestamp and random generation. The change avoids BigInt overhead by combining two 32-bit integers (timestamp, random) into a 64-bit hex string before converting to base64url. Internal refactor; ID format and collision resistance remain functionally equivalent.

eli5.text: The system that creates short, unique IDs for messages now generates the random part of those IDs using simpler math that runs directly on regular numbers instead of special big-number calculations. If you glanced at how these IDs are made, you’d notice the code no longer handles extra-large integers when building them. The IDs still look the same and stay just as unlikely to clash with each other, but they’re produced with a lighter, faster process that doesn’ need the overhead of big-number math.

ai.title: Bump npm-app version to 1.0.328
ai.summary: Version bumped from 1.0.327 to 1.0.328 in `npm-app/package.json`. Routine release increment. No functional changes.

eli5.text: The assistant now generates short, unique IDs using 64-bit base64url encoding, producing identifiers roughly 11 characters long instead of longer formats. These compact IDs are created whenever the system needs to label a checkpoint or save a session state, making references shorter and easier to read. Updating to this version is live today and takes effect automatically for anyone using the latest build, so you will see IDs like 'a1b2c3d4e5F' appear in checkpoint logs or save prompts where longer sequences used to show up.

ai.title: evals: switch APIBASE to prod, lower concurrency
ai.summary: In evals/git-evals/run-eval-set.ts, API_BASE changed from localhost:3000 to https://www.codebuff.com/. Global concurrency limit reduced from 10 to 5. Affects eval set execution only.

eli5.text: The software that runs the test suites used to send all its test traffic to a local copy on your own computer (http://localhost:3000/), and now it sends that traffic to the real, public website (https://www.codebuff.com/). On top of that, the test runner was told to do fewer things at the same time - it used to juggle 10 tasks simultaneously, and now it only juggles 5. If you looked, you would see the test logs reporting responses from the live site rather than a local server, and the runs would progress more slowly because half as many tasks are running in parallel.

ai.title: Buffbench page update and admin visibility controls
ai.summary: Added PATCH /api/git-evals/visibility route for admins to toggle eval result public status. Refactored admin email constants into common/src/constants.ts. Updated web/src/app/evals/page.tsx with session-aware admin checks and new visibility UI controls. Requires admin session for visibility changes.

eli5.text: Admins on the Evals page can now click a control next to each benchmark result to make it publicly viewable or hide it from public view without deleting it. The new visibility toggle checks that you are logged in as an admin (the same people who already manage the system) before letting you flip the public/not-public switch for any result. Behind the scenes, the list of who counts as an admin was consolidated into one shared place so future admin-only features use the same definition, and the extra metrics shown on each result (average completion and code-quality numbers) now update correctly. If you are not an admin, nothing on the page changes for you today.

The assistant no longer tells itself that earlier replies came from a dumber AI and then quietly rewrites them to look like its own work. If you watched a long back-and-forth, you’d just see the same assistant staying consistent from start to finish instead of subtly editing its own past messages. Internal staff who handle how the assistant builds its replies are the only ones this affects, and it’s already live today.

ai.title: Main prompt removes previous assistant correction instruction
ai.summary: Removed the self-correction instruction that framed prior assistant messages as from a less intelligent assistant from `mainPrompt` in `backend/src/main-prompt.ts`, with `expireMessages` history now passed through without `castAssistantMessage` mapping. The change is scoped to backend prompt construction, commenting out the `hasAssistantMessage`-gated `user` instruction with `timeToLive: 'userPrompt'`. The `castAssistantMessage` import was removed while `expireMessages(messageHistory, 'userPrompt' | 'agentStep')` selection is preserved.
